"Your hands are shaking," Shankar said in the corridor outside the viva room.
"I know. Look." Madhav held one up and turned it over. "Palms wet too. I've revised for weeks and my body still thinks I'm being chased."
"That's just adrenaline. My brother says it means you're ready."
"Ready to faint?"
Shankar laughed. "Ready to talk. Try this: press your feet down on the floor and breathe out slowly. And say your first sentence in your head."
Madhav did it. His shoulders lowered a little. "My first sentence is 'The main finding is...' Right."
The examiner called his name.
"Go," Shankar said. "Tell me after. If it feels like this all the time, talk to the counsellor."

passage: I'm Jomon, and I used to think my shaking hands before a speech meant I was bad at speaking. In my final year the department picked me to give the welcome speech. The evening before, my palms were so damp the paper stuck to them. My friend Avni found me pacing the courtyard. She didn't tell me to stop being nervous. She said, "Your body's getting you ready. Practise once for me, standing." I did, and my voice wobbled, and she told me the first line was strong. On the day I pressed my feet flat, breathed out and looked at the back wall. My hands still shook a little. But I finished, and the nerves felt more like energy than like danger.

Speech coach's note, college public speaking club, Wednesday.
Hrithik gave his first competition speech today. Before he went on, I saw his hands shaking so much the cue cards rattled, and he kept wiping his palms on his trousers. He told me, "I'm going to mess this up. My body's telling me I'm not ready." I said, "Your body's telling you this matters. That's energy. Let's use it." We did three slow breaths together, feet flat on the floor, and I asked him to squeeze his fists and release them. He walked on still a little shaky, but his first line came out strong. By the second minute his hands had steadied. His teammate Vishal told me afterwards that Hrithik has been having these shakes before every small class presentation, not just big events, and sometimes can't sleep the night before. I've suggested he talk to the college counsellor as well, and he's agreed to go on Friday.
— Coach Ananya

qa.a: His trousers.

qa.a: He was very nervous, sure he'd mess up, with shaking hands and damp palms.

qa.q: What helped Hrithik steady himself?
qa.a: Reframing the shakes as energy, slow breaths with feet flat, and squeezing and releasing his fists.

qa.q: What did Vishal notice about Hrithik's nerves?
qa.a: Vishal noticed the shakes happen before every small presentation and sometimes stop him sleeping, which is why counselling was suggested.

Tuesday night.
Viva tomorrow at ten. My hands have been shaking since dinner. I spilled half my tea. Jyoti saw and laughed kindly and said, "Nerves?" I said it felt like my body was betraying me.
She told me something her sports coach said: the same shaky, sweaty feeling comes before a race and before a panic, and you can decide which it is. "Tell yourself: my body's getting ready." I rolled my eyes, but I tried it. It sort of helped.
We went through my three hardest questions one more time. I wrote my opening line on a card. Then I did the breathing thing: in for four, out for six, feet on the floor.
Still shaky. But less. Going to sleep now.
If this keeps happening before every exam, Jyoti says I should talk to the counsellor, and I think I will.
— Kishore

passage: In the corridor outside the practical exam hall at the nursing college in Kolar, Ishita's hands would not stop shaking. Her palms were so damp she wiped them on her white coat twice. "I'm going to drop the thermometer," she whispered. Nirmala, a final-year student volunteering that day, sat beside her on the bench. "Your heart's racing because your body's getting ready," she said. "It's the same feeling as excitement. Tell yourself, 'I'm ready,' not 'I'm scared.'" She showed Ishita how to press both feet into the floor and name five things she could see: the peeling green paint, the fan, the notice about bus timings, a crow on the window, her own name on the list. Ishita's breathing slowed. "Does it ever stop?" she asked. "Mostly it gets smaller," Nirmala said. "If it ever turns into panic that won't settle, even on ordinary days, the college counsellor is good. I went in my second year." Then Ishita's name was called.

qa.q: How many things did Nirmala ask Ishita to name?
qa.a: Five things she could see.

qa.q: What was Ishita worried about in the corridor?
qa.a: Ishita felt anxious that her shaking hands would make her drop the thermometer in the exam.

qa.q: Which tools did Nirmala offer?
qa.a: Reframing the racing heart as readiness, pressing the feet into the floor, naming five things in sight, and the counsellor if panic ever keeps coming back.

qa.q: How did Nirmala seem to see Ishita's nerves?
qa.a: As a normal sign of the body getting ready, something Nirmala had felt too, not a weakness.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult with shaky hands and damp palms before a practical exam, easing it with grounding and reframing, with professional support for persistent panic.
